name: Sumbawa, Sumbawa Besar dialect
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Shiohara, Asako. 2013. Tense, aspect, mood and polarity in the Sumbawa Besar dialect of Sumbawa. In John Bowden (ed.), Tense, aspect, mood and evidentiality in languages of Indonesia. NUSA 55: 173-192. hdl:10108/74332. Corroborated: Shiohara, Asako. 2014. Deixis in the Sumbawa Besar dialect of Sumbawa. NUSA 56: 139-152 (p.142), and Shiohara, Asako. 2013. Voice in the Sumbawa Besar dialect of Sumbawa. NUSA 54: 145-158 (fn.4, sec.3.2).
catalog_locator: NUSA 55 p.175, section 2 'Predicate structure and constituent indicating TAM', paragraph 'The phonological property of each category..' and footnote 4; p.176 on ka/ma/na and the negators Corroboration: NUSA 56 p.142 (section 1) and NUSA 54 p.148 fn.4, p.152 sec.3.2.
catalog_quote: The phonological property of each category is as follows. In Sumbawa, the stress is located on the final syllable of each word (e.g., kawa ‘coffee’, nginom ‘drink’, in which stressed syllables are underlined) 4. A subject prefix and an AM clitic are always pronounced without stress. The former is attached to the predicate head (e.g., ku-laló ‘I go’, sia-kakan ‘you eat’), while the latter may phonologically attach to the subsequent constituent, if any, to form a stress unit. ... The past tense marker ka and the mood marker ma ‘request, invitation’ are not normally stressed. ... However, these markers are stressed when followed by an AM marker. ... The negators (nó and siong) and the mood marker na ‘polite prohibition’ are always stressed. [fn.4] Some words are lexically stressed more strongly than other words, and in some cases, the existence or absence of such stress may cause a distinction in meaning. Such stronger lexical stress is indicated by an apostrophe, as in the following examples: tunóng’ ‘sleep’ tunóng ‘burn’ popo’ ‘make a magic’ popo ‘wash’ [NUSA 56 p.142] In Sumbawa, word-level stress is located on the final syllable of each word (for example, kawa ‘coffee’ and nginom ‘drink’, in which the stressed syllables are underlined). A stressed syllable is pronounced longer and louder than other syllables. The clitics ku, mu, tu are, however, pronounced without stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the word (stressed syllable longer and louder per NUSA 56 p.142). Pronominal subject proclitics/genitive enclitics, aspect-mood clitics, future ya, and (normally) past ka and invitational ma are unstressed and join an adjacent word in one stress unit whose single stress is on the unit's last syllable; negators nó, siong and prohibitive na are always stressed. No weight or vowel-quality conditions are stated.
new_statements.exceptions: A lexical class of words carries 'stronger than usual' final stress, occasionally meaning-distinguishing (tunóng' vs tunóng, popo' vs popo), written with a word-final apostrophe; Shiohara 2009 (AALL 4, pp.78-79) adds that on words ending in an open syllable or -ng this may surface as a glottal stop or falling pitch depending on syntactic position, and Shiohara 2025 (AALL 19) rewrites these words with a final phonemic glottal stop /ʔ/. Clitics are stressless; in purposive serial verbs and undergoer incorporation the first element loses its stress and the whole unit carries one final stress (AALL 1 p.47; NUSA 54 sec.3.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word, extended to a 'stress unit' (word plus clitics/demonstratives, incorporated V+N, SVC V1+V2) whose single stress falls on the unit-final syllable; statements are based on conversational field data from the Sumbawa Besar dialect, impressionistic (no instrumental study).
new_statements.identity_note: All of Shiohara's statements describe the Sumbawa Besar dialect (data from Sumbawa Besar town and Empang, central Sumbawa), which she says serves as the inter-dialect lingua franca; the other dialects (Taliwang, Jereweh, Tongo) are not covered. Glottolog language-level code sumb1241 applies; dialect-level code not verified.

tone.quote: Materi ini menyajikan beberapa hal yaitu, jenis fonem bahasa Sumbawa dan sistem pelambangannya. Seperti bahasa lainnya, bahasa Sumbawa memiliki bunyi vocal dan konsonan. Terdapat 29 bunyi atau fonem dalam bahasa Sumbawa, yaitu 10 bunyi vokal dan 19 bunyi konsonan (/p/, /b/, /t/, /d/, /c/, /j/, /k/, /g/, /q/, /s/, /h/, /m/, /n/, /ñ/, //, /r/, /l/, /w/, dan /y/). Dengan menggunakan prinsip-prinsip pelambangan bunyi bahasa atau ejaan di atas, dijelaskan bahwa bunyi vokal dilambangkan dengan 7 huruf, yaitu <i, e, ē, u, o, ō, dan a>, sedangkan bunyi konsonan dilambangkan dengan 18 huruf <p, b, t, d, c, j, k, g, s, q, h, m, r, l, w, y, ny, dan ng>.
tone.locator: p.227, section 'Hasil dan pembahasan', paragraph on Materi kedua 'Sistem Ejaan Bahasa Sumbawa'; the generic 'intonasi, lafal, dan tekanan' dialect remark is on p.223, section 'Latar belakang'.
tone.translation: This material presents several points, namely the types of phonemes of Sumbawa and the system for symbolizing them. Like other languages, Sumbawa has vowel and consonant sounds. There are 29 sounds or phonemes in Sumbawa, namely 10 vowel sounds and 19 consonant sounds (/p/, /b/, /t/, /d/, /c/, /j/, /k/, /g/, /q/, /s/, /h/, /m/, /n/, /ñ/, // [a glyph, evidently the velar nasal, is lost in the PDF text layer], /r/, /l/, /w/ and /y/). Using the principles for symbolizing speech sounds or spelling above, it is explained that the vowel sounds are symbolized with 7 letters, i, e, ē, u, o, ō and a, while the consonant sounds are symbolized with 18 letters p, b, t, d, c, j, k, g, s, q, h, m, r, l, w, y, ny and ng.
